newsitem.title: UK: Nobility at a price, lordships go under the hammer.
newsitem.headline: Nobility at a price, lordships go under the hammer.

text.p: It might just be the perfect accessory for that up-and-comer who has everything -- an aristocratic title with a thousand-year history.
To some, purchasing an ancient pedigree is the ultimate sign of success while to others, any attempt at buying in to nobility reeks of tackiness and the nouveau riche.

But for 26 people who splashed out a total of nearly 400,000 pounds ($663,000) at an auction of manorial titles in London on Wednesday, it means they may now call themselves lords and ladies, whatever anyone might think.

The Manorial Society of Great Britain holds three to four such auctions per year where down-and-out aristocrats or those simply tired of carrying so many lordships as a birthright can sell some of their ancient titles.
"We think of it as a service for our members," explained Robert Smith, chairman of the grouping of British title-holders.
"These things have always been bought and sold, dating back as far as William the Conqueror and the Doomsday Book in 1086."
The Barony of Houston netted almost 100,000 pounds in the auction from an anonymous buyer wanting to become the new baron or baroness of the rural Scottish village.

The manorships and baronies have long since had any feudal powers associated with them stripped away by legislation. Gone are such powerful rights as forcing serfs to work the land or dispensing justice with such whimsical commands as 'Off with his head!'.

While Britain still has hereditary peers who sit in the House of Lords, the country's upper chamber of parliament, purchased titles do not include any such ancient privilege nor do they convey noble status.

The buyers must now content themselves with nothing more than an elaborate sheet of paper certifying them as the bearer of the titles, which have long since had any accompanying estate or castle stripped away.
"But it might well help us to get a dinner reservation somewhere," said the new Lord of Chuderleigh, who entered the auction room as plain Michael Soloman.
He and his wife Jennifer purchased a manorship in their home county of Devonshire for 7,500 pounds. "It's all in good fun. We won't use it too often."

Many of the titles are sold by aristocrats facing enormous death duties or other bills for maintaining their family estates. Last year, for example, Princess Diana's brother sold the Lordship of Wimbledon for 188,000 pounds to redo the plumbing at his stately home.
One man looking slightly ill at ease at the back of the overflowing auction room confessed that several of the titles for sale were his, though he declined to name which ones.
"I inherited them, but they haven't any particular significance for me," he said, adding that he still had a few lordships to spare.
Among the day's newly titled were Bill and Dawn Rice, who spent 6,350 pounds for the right to call themselves Lord and Lady of Ballynacathy. They saw their purchase as a shrewd business decision.
"We run two wedding shops so we thought it might be good for business. You know, 'Want to be lord for a day, then why not be chauffeured to the church by a real lord?' That kind of thing."
Most of the buyers who attend the Manorial Society's quarterly sales tend to be British, with an occasional continental European and American.

"They tend to be well-heeled, self-made folk -- very much like their predecessors really, just a different kind of robber baron," Smith said. "You obviously get flashy types...There is always someone where you think 'Oh god they don't deserve it', but of course they've got the money."

As if as a warning to any such buyer, the auctioneers had set up several tables with literature of potential interest to the new title holders. Scattered among the books was one aptly titled "The Natural History of Stuck-up People." ($ = 0.602 British Pounds)
